Arizona is the clear pick based on the profiles given. The biggest matchup driver is physical advantage at both ends. Arizona is built around size, paint scoring, offensive rebounding, and foul pressure, averaging 86.1 points, 42.5 rebounds, 19.1 made free throws, and 434 offensive rebounds in 34 games, while holding opponents to 39.2% shooting. LIU is a well-coached, veteran underdog, but its own report explicitly notes that elite size and pace can distort it, with the Illinois blowout and the Mississippi State game serving as warnings against high-major athleticism and frontcourt strength. Arizona’s front line of Motiejus Krivas and Tobe Awaka, plus the rebounding and mismatch help from Koa Peat, is exactly the kind of interior pressure that threatens LIU’s structure.

Arizona’s offense is also a difficult stylistic problem for LIU. The Wildcats do not need hot three-point shooting to separate; they want possessions to end at the rim, at the foul line, or through second chances. That is dangerous against an LIU team whose defensive identity is solid but whose statistical profile still allowed 44.5% shooting overall. LIU has rim protection from Shadrak Lasu and good hands from Greg Gordon, but Arizona’s volume of interior attacks is much heavier than what LIU typically sees in NEC play. Awaka’s 125 offensive rebounds, Krivas’s 58.2% shooting, and the downhill creation from Jaden Bradley and Brayden Burries suggest Arizona can win the shot-quality battle even if the game is played in the half court. Bradley’s 154 assists and Arizona’s ability to flow from ball screen to duck-in to offensive rebound also indicate the Wildcats are unlikely to be solved by one defensive look.

On the other side, LIU does have qualities that could keep the game respectable for stretches. Fuller, Davis, and Gordon form a legitimate veteran scoring core, and LIU is comfortable in close games. The Sharks can shorten the game, execute in the half court, and make smart use of Fuller’s face-up scoring and Davis’s late-clock shot creation. They also defend the three well enough on paper, allowing 31.9% from deep, and Arizona is not a high-volume perimeter team anyway. But that actually pushes the game toward Arizona’s preferred terms rather than away from them. If LIU takes away some catch-and-shoot rhythm, Arizona is still happy to pound the paint, attack the glass, and live at the line.

The decisive edge is Arizona’s defensive profile against LIU’s offensive style. LIU is most effective when it can play selective, efficient half-court basketball through post touches, cuts, and ball screens. Arizona defends that kind of offense very well with length and positioning, holding opponents to 39.2% overall and 31.4% from three, with Krivas protecting the rim and Awaka finishing possessions on the glass. The Wildcats do not need to gamble; they can stay in shell, crowd the paint, and force LIU into tougher late-clock looks. LIU’s offense is efficient, but it is not built on high-volume threes or overwhelming shot creation, which means Arizona’s interior defense and rebounding should be able to gradually squeeze possessions.

Coaching and résumé also favor Arizona. Tommy Lloyd has repeatedly guided Arizona deep into March, with three Sweet 16 runs in four prior seasons, and his 2025-26 team has documented high-end wins over Houston, Baylor, Kansas, Iowa State, and Alabama. LIU has had an excellent NEC season under Rod Strickland and shows real poise, but this is his first NCAA tournament appearance as a head coach. Arizona has already proven it can win both track meets and rock fights against elite competition; LIU’s best path is to make this a tense, lower-possession game, but Arizona has already shown it can beat top teams in exactly that environment.

Overall, LIU’s discipline and veteran guards may allow it to compete early, but Arizona’s superior size, rebounding, rim pressure, defensive length, and battle-tested backcourt should control the game over 40 minutes. The most likely script is LIU hanging around while it can execute in the half court, then Arizona creating separation through second-chance points, free throws, and sustained defensive pressure in the paint.

Arizona should win this matchup based on a clear edge in team quality, physicality, and proven performance against elite competition. The Wildcats’ profile is that of a national-title-caliber high seed: 32-2 overall, Big 12 regular-season and tournament champions, 86.1 points per game, 50.2% shooting, 42.5 rebounds per game, and opponents held to 68.8 points on 39.2% shooting. LIU, by contrast, looks like a respectable but limited low-major auto-bid: 24-10, NEC champion, NET No. 198, SRS -4.75, 108.3 offensive rating, 104.0 defensive rating, and a very weak strength of schedule. The broad statistical gap strongly favors Arizona.

The most important matchup factor is Arizona’s interior dominance versus an LIU team whose profile does not suggest it can withstand high-major size. Arizona’s offense is built around rim pressure, post play, offensive rebounding, and foul drawing. The Wildcats make 19.1 free throws per game, collected 434 offensive rebounds in 34 games, and feature multiple frontcourt weapons in Motiejus Krivas and Tobe Awaka, plus slashers and mismatch scorers like Brayden Burries and Koa Peat. LIU’s report describes a defense-first mid-major with some competence, but also notes that the Sharks were substantially overmatched by high-major physicality, length, and half-court defense in games against teams like Illinois, Notre Dame, and others. That is a major warning sign here, because Arizona’s greatest strength is exactly the kind of physical pressure that has already given LIU trouble.

Arizona also has the more reliable offensive creation. Jaden Bradley organizes the attack with 154 assists and is effective in high ball screens and paint-touch creation, Burries is the lead scorer and late-clock shot maker, and Dell’Orso provides proven scoring punch off the bench. That variety matters against a team like LIU that appears better defensively than offensively. Even if LIU can slow the game for stretches, Arizona has multiple pathways to efficient offense: post entries, second-chance points, free throws, and inside-out looks. LIU’s offense, meanwhile, is only modest by the available metrics, with an offensive rating of 108.3 that ranks around the low-middle national tier. Against Arizona’s length-and-positioning defense, which holds opponents to 39.2% overall and 31.4% from three, LIU may struggle to generate enough scoring to keep up.

Defensively, Arizona is also well equipped to erase the kind of balanced-but-not-explosive attack LIU brings. The Wildcats do not need to gamble heavily; they protect the paint with Krivas, finish possessions with rebounding through Awaka and others, and have disruptive perimeter defenders in Burries, Bradley, and Kharchenkov. LIU’s profile explicitly says it is not a high-octane underdog built to bomb away. That is significant because Arizona’s clearest vulnerability from the report is against teams that survive the paint battle and force the Wildcats into perimeter shot-making contests, as Texas Tech did with 11 made threes. LIU does not appear to fit that archetype. Instead, the Sharks look more ordinary offensively and more dependent on steadiness than explosive shot-making, which plays directly into Arizona’s defensive strengths.

The résumé comparison further widens the gap. Arizona has major wins over Alabama, Houston, Kansas, Baylor, BYU, and Iowa State, and repeatedly demonstrated the ability to beat elite teams in different styles, including both up-tempo and grind-it-out games. LIU’s résumé suggests success mostly within a weak NEC environment, with a No. 326 strength of schedule and clear struggles when stepping up in class. A team with a NET of 198 and that schedule profile generally needs a very specific upset formula; nothing in the reports suggests LIU has a distinct tactical edge that would offset Arizona’s overwhelming advantages in talent, size, rebounding, and battle-tested execution.

Arizona’s late-game and coaching profile also favor the Wildcats. Tommy Lloyd’s team has shown the ability to adjust during games, flip second halves with defense and shot selection, and close with free throws. Lloyd also has a strong NCAA track record at Arizona, with three Sweet 16 runs in four prior seasons. LIU’s report is more about statistical respectability than demonstrated top-end scalability. The Sharks may be able to make the game uncomfortable briefly if they defend well and control tempo, but over 40 minutes Arizona’s superior frontcourt force, rebounding volume, paint scoring, and defensive size should wear them down.

In short, this looks like a classic high-seed versus credible but overmatched low-major matchup. LIU has enough defensive structure to avoid looking fraudulent, but Arizona is stronger in every decisive area: interior scoring, offensive rebounding, foul pressure, shot creation, defense, depth, and quality of opposition faced. Based solely on the provided analyses, Arizona is the clear pick.

Arizona is the clear pick based on the matchup described in the two reports. The biggest deciding factor is Arizona’s overwhelming frontcourt size, rebounding, and interior physicality against the exact type of weakness LIU is said to have. That is a direct problem for LIU, whose analysis specifically says the Sharks can be punished by true power-conference size, especially at the 4/5 spots, with Lasu productive but undersized at 6-8/200 and Miranda not a major-minute anchor. The LIU report explicitly says that a team with a legit 6-9 or 6-10 scorer who can finish through contact can target their frontcourt physically, force help rotations, and create foul trouble. Arizona also matches up well with LIU’s offensive style. LIU’s offense is creator-led rather than system-led, leaning on Davis, Fuller, Gordon, and Goings to win first actions off the dribble. Arizona’s defense is almost custom-built for that: disciplined shell principles, elite size behind the ball, opponents held to 39.2% overall and 31.4% from three, and a philosophy of crowding the paint without over-rotating. Krivas protects the rim, Awaka finishes possessions on the glass, and the perimeter trio of Burries, Bradley, and Kharchenkov provides point-of-attack disruption without gambling recklessly. Since LIU is less comfortable in long half-court possessions against size and physicality—as shown in the losses to Fordham and Illinois—Arizona’s defensive structure attacks the exact pressure points identified in the scouting report.

Another major edge is turnover and possession control. Arizona already thrives on turning mistakes into points, as seen in the Houston win where it turned 16 turnovers into 16 points. While Arizona is not described as a reckless full-court pressure team, it does have the personnel to disrupt LIU’s creators at the point of attack and then convert those disrupted possessions into transition or early-post offense. Against a team with a roughly even turnover margin and a 1.0 assist/turnover ratio, Arizona’s discipline and length should create extra possessions.

The pace and game-script dynamics also favor Arizona. LIU is most dangerous when games either settle into a manageable physical rhythm against similar-size opponents or when the Sharks can string together momentum bursts off live-ball defense and early offense. Arizona is less likely to allow either comfort zone. The Wildcats can flatten LIU’s half-court offense by loading the paint and making them score late over size, and they can also run off misses and makes with early advance passes and drag screens, which the LIU report identifies as a way to neutralize the Sharks’ shot-blocking setup. Arizona’s own offense is powerful enough to dictate terms: if LIU tries to grind, Arizona has half-court size and execution; if the game opens up, Arizona has more talent, better interior finishers, and better depth.

Experience and proven high-level performance further separate the teams. Arizona owns wins over Houston, Baylor, Kansas, Iowa State, and Alabama, showing it can beat elite opponents in both rock fights and higher-end offensive games. LIU’s profile is strong within the NEC, but the report repeatedly notes that high-major size and physicality caused major problems in losses to Illinois, Georgia, and Mississippi State. LIU does have some paths to competitiveness. Fuller’s shooting, Gordon’s all-around play, and the team’s sturdy 2/3/4-line physicality could keep them from being overwhelmed on the perimeter, and if Arizona somehow lets the game become a perimeter shot-making contest—similar to the Texas Tech loss—LIU could hang around longer than expected. But the overall matchup points strongly the other way. Arizona’s biggest strength directly attacks LIU’s biggest weakness, and Arizona’s defensive style directly counters LIU’s preferred offensive creation model. Over 40 minutes, Arizona’s size, rebounding, rim defense, foul pressure, and high-major depth should wear LIU down and control the game.

Tempo is another edge for Arizona. LIU is comfortable winning games in the 60s or low 70s and would prefer to make this a possession-by-possession contest. If Arizona speeds the game up through transition flow, offensive rebounding, and physical rim pressure, LIU’s lack of depth and its prior issues against high-major athleticism become more dangerous. The LIU report explicitly says elite size and pace can distort them, and Arizona’s report describes exactly that kind of team: fast enough to magnify advantages, powerful enough to dominate the glass, and efficient enough to turn pace into separation.

LIU does bring qualities that could keep stretches competitive. Still, the reports point to a game that likely swings Arizona’s way as physical advantages accumulate. Arizona’s low-turnover offense should prevent LIU from manufacturing enough disruption, while Arizona’s rebounding and free-throw pressure should create extra possessions and efficient scoring opportunities. LIU’s biggest risk area from its own report is that when the half-court offense bogs down, the margin gets thin; against Arizona’s elite defense, that is likely to happen more often than it did in NEC play. In short, LIU has the traits of a dangerous and composed mid-major champion, but Arizona has too much top-end quality, too much interior force, too much schedule-proven two-way efficiency, and too favorable a style matchup. The most likely outcome based on these reports is Arizona imposing its size, rebounding, and defensive pressure, limiting LIU’s half-court comfort, and pulling away as the talent and physicality gap shows over 40 minutes.

Arizona is the stronger pick because LIU’s biggest vulnerabilities line up directly with Arizona’s clearest strengths. Arizona’s identity is paint volume, offensive rebounding, foul pressure, and transition scoring: 86.7 points per game, 50.2% shooting, 43.0 rebounds, 19.4 made free throws, a +11.6 rebounding margin, and 17.0 fastbreak points per game. The reports do identify a theoretical upset path against Arizona: pack the lane, force low-volume perimeter shooting, keep the rebounding margin close, hold them under 10 fastbreak points, and turn the game into a 65- to 68-possession half-court grinder. But based solely on these analyses, LIU is not an ideal opponent to pull that off. LIU’s defense has struggled when opponents repeatedly force floor-runs and when games get physically stretched, and Arizona is elite in exactly those high-leverage areas—transition bursts, offensive glass waves, and paint pressure. Even if LIU can crowd the lane at times, the concern is whether it has enough true size to finish possessions with rebounds and enough discipline to avoid sending Arizona to the foul line. Arizona has already shown it can win even without making many threes, because its offense is not built around perimeter volume in the first place.

There is also a talent-and-athleticism gap across positions. LIU does have strong, interchangeable wings and capable scorers in Fuller, Davis, Gordon, and Goings, so it is not without offensive answers, but the LIU report repeatedly suggests that high-major length and physicality can flatten its drive-first attack. Arizona’s defense allows only 68.6 points per game and 38.8% shooting, and its game plan against LIU would be clear: wall off first drives, force LIU east-west, and make those creators finish over length in crowded paint.

In short, LIU’s best attributes—physical wings, creator-led offense, and opportunistic transition off turnovers—do not attack Arizona’s core profile as effectively as Arizona’s strengths attack LIU’s weaknesses. Arizona’s rebounding dominance, frontcourt size, transition output, and foul pressure give it multiple ways to control the game, while LIU’s lack of proven interior heft against power opponents makes it difficult to see the Sharks consistently surviving Arizona’s paint pressure over 40 minutes. Based on the reports alone, Arizona is the more likely winner.
